subtopic_detail: Knee pain in an adolescent where the examination redirects the imaging
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 13 year old boy with three weeks of aching in the left knee that is worse after football training and eases with rest. There was no single injury and no swelling.

He weighs 78 kg and his body mass index sits above the 97th centile. He walks into the room with the left foot turned outwards. The left knee has full range of movement, no effusion, no joint line tenderness and stable ligaments. When you flex the left hip the thigh rolls into external rotation, and internal rotation of that hip is limited to 10 degrees compared with 40 degrees on the right. He is afebrile and systemically well.

data_table.Examination: Out toeing gait on the left, normal knee examination with no effusion, obligatory external rotation on left hip flexion, left hip internal rotation 10 degrees versus 40 degrees on the right
data_table.Growth: Weight 78 kg, body mass index above the 97th centile for age

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee within two weeks
options.rationale: Knee imaging follows a knee examination that is actually abnormal, and a full painless knee with restricted hip rotation makes the knee the referral site rather than the source (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Advise relative rest, ibuprofen and physiotherapy for the knee pain
options.rationale: Conservative management fits patellofemoral pain, which reproduces symptoms on patellar compression and squatting rather than restricting hip internal rotation (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Arrange left knee radiographs and review in the fracture clinic later
options.rationale: Films of the wrong joint are the usual reason for delayed diagnosis in this presentation, and the delay allows a stable slip to become unstable (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Order pelvis radiographs including frog leg views and refer urgently
options.rationale: Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion with loss of internal rotation in a heavy adolescent is the classical hip sign, and both anteroposterior and frog leg lateral views are needed because early slips are visible only on the lateral (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Check inflammatory markers and arrange an ultrasound of the left knee
options.rationale: Inflammatory markers and ultrasound target septic arthritis or an effusion, and three weeks of activity related pain in an afebrile boy with a dry knee does not fit that pattern (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp).

explanation.summary: Hip pathology in children and adolescents refers pain to the distal thigh and knee through the obturator nerve, and a substantial proportion of slipped capital femoral epiphysis presents with knee pain alone. The examination that redirects the diagnosis costs seconds: compare internal rotation of both hips with the patient supine and watch for obligatory external rotation as the hip is flexed. Delay converts a stable slip, in which the child can still weight bear, into an unstable slip with a markedly higher risk of avascular necrosis. Treatment is in situ screw fixation, and the contralateral hip is assessed at the same time because bilateral disease is common.
key_points: Examine the hips in every child or adolescent presenting with knee pain
Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion is the most specific bedside sign
Frog leg lateral views are required because early slips hide on the anteroposterior film
Keep the child non weight bearing once the diagnosis is suspected
Endocrine screening is considered in slips outside the usual age or weight range
explanation.pearls: Around one in five adolescents with a slipped capital femoral epiphysis presents with isolated knee or thigh pain, so a knee examination that is entirely normal should send the film request to the pelvis rather than the knee.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

subtopic_detail: Acute painful vulval swelling and the drainage technique that reduces recurrence
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department. A 27 year old woman presents with three days of increasing pain and swelling on the right side of the vaginal opening. She cannot sit down or walk comfortably and has not been able to sleep.

She is not pregnant, has no urinary symptoms and has had no previous similar episode. On examination there is a tense fluctuant swelling about 4 cm across in the posterior part of the right labium majus, distorting the introitus. The overlying skin is thin and shiny but the surrounding vulval and perineal skin is not indurated or discoloured, and there is no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.4
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant 4 cm swelling in the posterior right labium majus distorting the introitus, thin shiny overlying skin, no surrounding induration or crepitus
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Incise and drain under local anaesthetic and insert a Word catheter
options.rationale: Drainage relieves the pain immediately, and leaving a balloon catheter in place for several weeks allows a lined tract to epithelialise, which is what lowers the recurrence rate compared with simple incision (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Disorders; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin and metronidazole with twice daily warm baths
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone do not decompress a walled off collection, and they are added to drainage only when there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic upset or immunosuppression (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Aspirate the swelling with a wide bore needle and send fluid for culture
options.rationale: Needle aspiration empties the cavity but leaves no drainage tract, and the collection reaccumulates in a high proportion of women within weeks (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Disorders).

options.text: Arrange excision of the gland on the next elective gynaecology list
options.rationale: Excision is reserved for repeatedly recurrent disease because it carries bleeding, scarring and dyspareunia risks, and it does not address tonight's pain (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Disorders).

options.text: Refer for biopsy of the swelling to exclude an underlying malignancy
options.rationale: Biopsy at the time of drainage belongs to women over 40 or with a solid irregular mass, and an acutely fluctuant tender swelling in a woman of 27 does not meet that threshold (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Disorders).

explanation.summary: Obstruction of the duct of the greater vestibular gland produces a cyst that becomes an abscess when it is infected, and the organisms are usually mixed vaginal and enteric flora rather than a sexually transmitted pathogen. The therapeutic goal is not just to empty the cavity but to create a durable drainage tract, which is why a balloon tipped catheter or marsupialisation outperforms simple incision or aspiration. Antibiotics are an adjunct for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression. Age is the other decision point, because a vulval mass in a woman over 40 should prompt biopsy to exclude carcinoma of the gland.
key_points: Drainage plus a maintained tract is what prevents recurrence
A Word catheter is left in place for two to four weeks
Antibiotics are adjunctive, not a substitute for drainage
Simple incision or needle aspiration alone recurs frequently
Biopsy a vulval mass in a woman over 40 at the time of drainage
explanation.pearls: A Word catheter is left in for two to four weeks to epithelialise the tract, and removing it at the first review a week later is the common error that returns the woman to the emergency department.

subtopic_detail: Household varicella exposure in a seronegative woman in the second trimester
stem:
You are the antenatal clinic doctor. A 29 year old woman at 16 weeks in her second pregnancy telephones because her 4 year old daughter developed a widespread blistering rash two days ago and the general practitioner has diagnosed chickenpox. They share a bedroom while her partner works away.

She has never had chickenpox herself and has not been vaccinated. Her booking bloods, taken at 9 weeks, recorded varicella zoster immunoglobulin G as not detected. She feels completely well today, has no rash, no fever and no respiratory symptoms, and her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated with a normal first trimester ultrasound.

data_table.Examination: No rash on skin survey, chest clear, uterus palpable just below the umbilicus
data_table.Investigations: Booking varicella zoster immunoglobulin G not detected; rubella immunoglobulin G immune; hepatitis B surface antigen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give the live attenuated varicella vaccine and repeat serology in six weeks
options.rationale: Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy, and vaccination is instead offered in the postpartum period before discharge (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Start oral valaciclovir now and continue it until 21 days after exposure
options.rationale: Antiviral treatment is given if she develops the rash, and post exposure antiviral prophylaxis is a second line option only when immunoglobulin is unavailable or the window has closed (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Give varicella zoster immunoglobulin today and advise on warning symptoms
options.rationale: A seronegative pregnant woman with significant household contact should receive zoster immunoglobulin as soon as possible and within 96 hours where practicable, which both attenuates maternal disease and reduces the risk to the foetus (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Repeat varicella immunoglobulin G serology and act on the result next week
options.rationale: Serology has already been documented as negative in this pregnancy, and waiting for a repeat result consumes the narrow window in which immunoglobulin still works (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Reassure that the risk period has passed and review only if a rash appears
options.rationale: Congenital varicella syndrome risk extends across the first and second trimesters rather than ending at 12 weeks, so 16 weeks is still within the period of concern (Source: RANZCOG Infection in Pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Varicella in pregnancy carries two separate risks: severe maternal disease with pneumonitis, which is markedly more common in adults than children, and foetal infection. Congenital varicella syndrome complicates a small percentage of maternal infections occurring up to about 28 weeks, with the highest risk between 13 and 20 weeks. Zoster immunoglobulin given promptly after exposure to a seronegative woman attenuates maternal illness and is the intervention of choice, while aciclovir is used for treatment once a rash appears. Infection in the week before to the week after delivery is the separate neonatal emergency requiring immunoglobulin for the baby.
key_points: Check varicella serology at booking in women with no history of infection or vaccination
Zoster immunoglobulin is given as soon as possible after significant exposure
Live varicella vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy and given postpartum
Foetal risk continues into the second trimester rather than ending at 12 weeks
Maternal pneumonitis is the leading cause of severe maternal illness
explanation.pearls: Zoster immunoglobulin works best within 96 hours of exposure and can still be given up to 10 days, so the woman who telephones on day four is offered it that day rather than told she has missed the window.

subtopic_detail: Viral load threshold for antiviral prophylaxis to prevent perinatal hepatitis B transmission
stem:
You are the doctor in a hospital antenatal clinic reviewing a 31 year old woman at 26 weeks in her first pregnancy. Her booking bloods showed hepatitis B surface antigen positive, and she has known about her infection since a screening test in her teens but has never needed treatment.

She feels well, has no jaundice or abdominal pain, and takes no medication. Her liver is not enlarged and there are no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Her partner and her mother are both hepatitis B surface antigen positive. Foetal growth and liquor volume were normal on the morphology scan.

data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis B surface antigen positive; hepatitis B e antigen positive; hepatitis B virus DNA 3.2 x10^7 IU/mL; alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L (less than 35); bilirubin 9 micromol/L (less than 20); platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Examination: No hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly, no ascites or spider naevi

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to reduce transmission to her baby?

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean section at 39 weeks to reduce transmission
options.rationale: Mode of delivery does not reliably alter perinatal hepatitis B transmission, unlike the situation with untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection (Source: ASHM Hepatitis B in Pregnancy).

options.text: Rely on neonatal immunoglobulin and vaccine at birth without an antiviral
options.rationale: Immunoprophylaxis is given to every exposed newborn but still fails in up to one in ten babies of women with very high viral loads, which is the gap maternal antiviral therapy closes (Source: ASHM Hepatitis B in Pregnancy).

options.text: Start entecavir now and stop it at the onset of established labour
options.rationale: Entecavir lacks the pregnancy safety data of tenofovir and is not the agent chosen in this setting, and stopping at delivery risks a postpartum hepatitis flare (Source: ASHM Hepatitis B in Pregnancy).

options.text: Advise formula feeding from birth to reduce the risk of transmission
options.rationale: Breastfeeding is not a route of concern once the infant has received immunoglobulin and vaccine, and advising against it removes a benefit for no gain (Source: ASHM Hepatitis B in Pregnancy).

options.text: Start tenofovir disoproxil at 28 weeks and continue it after delivery
options.rationale: A maternal viral load above 200,000 IU/mL is the threshold for antiviral prophylaxis from about 28 to 32 weeks, and tenofovir is the agent with the best pregnancy safety data with monitoring for a flare after cessation (Source: ASHM Hepatitis B in Pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Perinatal transmission is the dominant route of chronic hepatitis B acquisition worldwide, and the risk tracks with maternal viral load rather than with symptoms or liver enzymes. Every infant born to a surface antigen positive woman receives hepatitis B immunoglobulin and the birth dose of vaccine within 12 hours, followed by the routine schedule and serological testing at nine months. Immunoprophylaxis alone fails in a meaningful proportion of babies when the maternal load is very high, so maternal antiviral therapy in the third trimester is added above the accepted threshold. The mother also needs ongoing hepatology follow up, since postpartum flares are common in the months after delivery.
key_points: Transmission risk is driven by maternal viral load, not by liver enzymes
Antiviral prophylaxis is indicated above 200,000 IU/mL
Tenofovir disoproxil is the preferred agent in pregnancy
Every exposed newborn gets immunoglobulin plus vaccine within 12 hours of birth
Test the infant serologically at nine months to confirm protection
explanation.pearls: Alanine aminotransferase can be entirely normal in a woman with a viral load above 10 million IU/mL, so the decision to start tenofovir at 28 weeks rests on the hepatitis B virus DNA result and not on liver function tests.

subtopic_detail: Counselling and timing at 41 weeks in an uncomplicated first pregnancy
stem:
You are the doctor in the antenatal clinic seeing a 30 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 41 weeks and 0 days. Her dates were confirmed by a crown rump length measurement at 9 weeks.

The pregnancy has been uncomplicated, with normal growth on clinical assessment and normal foetal movements reported today. The foetus is cephalic with the head engaged, the cardiotocograph is normal, and vaginal examination gives a Bishop score of 4. She tells you she has been reading about induction and would prefer to wait for labour to start by itself, and she asks what you would do in her position.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 112/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8, foetal heart rate 140
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 39 cm, cephalic presentation with the head engaged, cervix 1 cm dilated, 1 cm long, mid position, soft, station minus 2
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph normal with baseline 140 and moderate variability, no decelerations

options.text: Arrange twice weekly cardiotocography and fluid assessment until 42+6
options.rationale: Surveillance beyond 42 weeks does not prevent the rise in stillbirth and neonatal morbidity that accrues in that fortnight, and Australian practice offers birth before then (Source: RANZCOG Prolonged Pregnancy).

options.text: Offer a membrane sweep today and book induction before 42+0 weeks
options.rationale: Sweeping the membranes increases the chance of spontaneous labour and reduces the need for formal induction, and booking birth before 42 weeks respects both her preference and the rising perinatal risk (Source: RANZCOG Prolonged Pregnancy).

options.text: Admit her today for prostaglandin induction whatever her preference is
options.rationale: Induction at 41 weeks and 0 days is offered rather than imposed, and overriding an informed preference when there are several days of safe window is not justified (Source: RANZCOG Prolonged Pregnancy).

options.text: Recommend an elective caesarean section given the unfavourable cervix
options.rationale: A Bishop score of 4 predicts a longer induction rather than a failed one, and caesarean without an obstetric indication exposes her to surgical risk in this and later pregnancies (Source: RANZCOG Prolonged Pregnancy).

options.text: Review her in one week and reassess only if she has not laboured then
options.rationale: Deferring the conversation to 42 weeks removes the option of a planned induction within the recommended window and leaves her without foetal surveillance in the interval (Source: RANZCOG Prolonged Pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Perinatal mortality begins to climb from about 41 weeks and rises more steeply beyond 42 weeks, which is why Australian guidance offers induction between 41 and 42 weeks rather than waiting indefinitely. The counselling should present the absolute rather than the relative risk, since the numbers are small and the woman is entitled to weigh them. Membrane sweeping is a low cost intervention that brings forward spontaneous labour and reduces the proportion of women who need formal induction. If a woman declines induction after full discussion, the fallback is increased surveillance with a documented plan and a date for review rather than discharge from the pathway.
key_points: Induction is offered between 41 and 42 weeks in uncomplicated pregnancy
Membrane sweeping reduces the need for formal induction
A Bishop score below 6 predicts a longer induction, not a failed one
Present absolute risk figures when counselling about prolonged pregnancy
Document a surveillance plan if induction is declined
explanation.pearls: Stillbirth risk approximately doubles between 41 and 42 completed weeks even though it remains low in absolute terms, and quoting that as events per thousand rather than as a doubling is what allows a genuine choice.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Induction of Labour
